page.title: tinyactors compared with XState
page.description: Where a statechart runs, what format it is written in, what keeps a population of actors, how a running actor takes new logic, and when XState is the better choice.

hero.headline: Statecharts for a whole population of actors
hero.lede: XState gives you a machine and an actor in JavaScript, and leaves storing them to your code. tinyactors runs W3C SCXML charts as actors that hibernate, move to new versions and snapshot, in Node.js, Python, C and browsers. Choose XState for state in a JavaScript user interface.

section.heading: XState machines are JavaScript; SCXML is a standard
section.p: Both describe behavior as states, events and transitions, so a reviewer, a test or an agent can read the whole flow. The difference is the material.

claim.p: Stately calls XState a state management and orchestration solution for JavaScript and TypeScript apps. A machine is made with createMachine.
XState v6, in beta, reads SCXML through an experimental @xstate/scxml. Its tests are "regression coverage, not a claim of full SCXML conformance".
Each chart is a W3C SCXML document, and the C core passes all 191 automatic tests of the W3C conformance suite.
Every package runs the same suite, so a chart means the same thing in each language.
claim.source: Memory, capacity and performance, "Correct by the standard"

section.p: A document is data, so tools other than your program read it. The command line checks, lints and diffs a chart in CI, and draws it.

section.heading: One chart in four languages
section.p: XState runs, in Stately's words, "in the frontend, backend, or wherever JavaScript runs" (Stately, "XState"). tinyactors runs one C core behind each package.
This order retries a failed charge on its own. The same order.scxml runs in Node.js, a browser, Python and C, and each prints the same lines:

section.heading: XState persists one actor; the host, thousands
section.p: Ten thousand chat sessions, most of them idle, must survive until their users return. Something must pick which stay in memory.

claim.statement: XState hands you a snapshot to store
claim.p: actor.getPersistedSnapshot() returns an actor's state, with its children, and createActor(logic, {snapshot}) restores it.
Storing it is your application's work, in localStorage or a database, and it must be JSON-serializable.

claim.statement: The host hibernates the actors past a bound
claim.p: Give the host a store and a bound, and it writes the coldest actors into the store, then wakes each one at its next event.
Two million actors ran with at most 1000 in memory. One snapshot of two million takes 165 MB.
claim.source: Hibernation, "Run two million actors with 1000 in memory"
Snapshots, "Copy a running application, and run the copy"

section.p: An actor in memory takes about 530 bytes of a Node.js process holding a million, measured with a counter chart of one variable ().

section.heading: Both test the chart without the world
section.p: XState is stronger in one place. It generates test paths from a machine, where tinyactors leaves generated runs to your test.

claim.statement: XState mocks effects and generates paths
claim.p: Stately's docs say to mock a machine's effects, through setup(), to keep tests deterministic.
getShortestPaths returns a path to every reachable state, and Stately Studio generates tests from them for Playwright and Vitest.

claim.statement: A tinyactors chart's effects are events
claim.p: A chart reaches the world only through sends to objects you give the host, so a test gives it stand-ins. A simulated clock jumps to each timeout.
Properties over generated runs are a pattern your test writes, not a library call.
claim.source: Testing, "Replace the chart's services and its clock"

section.heading: A crash keeps what was written down
section.p: A process dies with sessions in flight. Neither library writes anything down on its own; the difference is how much your program has to write.

claim.statement: XState restores state, not the actions
claim.p: A restored actor does not run again the actions it already executed. For those, Stately's docs recommend event sourcing.

claim.statement: A crash keeps what your program saved
claim.p: Hibernated actors in your store and the last snapshot come back, with each actor's queued events and pending timers.
Inputs after that snapshot return when your program journaled them: replaying a journal is one loop.
claim.source: When to use tinyactors, "A crash stops memory and keeps saved state"

section.heading: Ship new rules to running sessions
section.p: You add a turn limit while thousands of sessions are mid-conversation. Each one must keep the turns it already counted.

claim.statement: XState's restored state may not fit new logic
claim.p: Stately's docs warn that if the machine changes, a restored state may be incompatible with the new logic.

claim.statement: A migration moves running actors to a version
claim.p: host.addImage() adds the new chart to the running host, and host.migrate() moves actors to it.
Each keeps its active states, queue and delayed sends. The new chart reads the old variables from one event.
claim.source: Migration, "Move the actors and carry their variables"

section.p: Ten thousand agent sessions answer three prompts each, with at most 100 in memory. Version 2 adds a limit of three turns, and one migration moves every session, hibernated ones included:
Version 2 read turns from the upgrade event. So every session ended at the limit instead of asking the model again.

section.heading: Choose tinyactors for actors on a server

item.term: Many long-lived actors, most of them waiting
item.text: The host hibernates them into your store, migrates them and snapshots them all.
One C core runs the same chart in Node.js, Python, C and browsers.
A W3C SCXML document, checked by the core against the W3C suite, outlives any one library.
An uploaded chart runs in the QuickJS sandbox, where a runaway loop ends in an error.

section.heading: Choose XState for logic in a JavaScript app

item.text: @xstate/react gives hooks such as useMachine, which runs an actor for the component's lifetime.
Stately Studio models machines visually, simulates them and exports the code into your codebase.
The graph utilities and Studio generate test paths from a machine; in tinyactors a generated run is code you write.
XState's actors can be promises, callbacks or observables too. A tinyactors actor always runs a chart.
XState v5 is current, and v6 is in beta. tinyactors is at 0.x and makes frequent breaking changes.
